care: Plutarch’s lives include wars, plots and violent deaths, told plainly but without much gore. This lesson summarizes those parts. The stories of Alexander and his horse, Solon and the rich king, Aristides “the Just” and Demosthenes practicing his speeches are good places for young readers to start.

young.html: Plutarch was a Greek who lived about 1,900 years ago, when Greece was part of the Roman Empire. He wrote short life stories of famous people. He put them in pairs, one Greek and one Roman, so readers could compare them: who was braver, who was wiser, who was fairer.
Plutarch cared most about character: what a person is like inside. He said that a small thing, like a joke or a quick answer, can show more about someone than a great battle.

Here is one of his stories. A wild horse named Bucephalus was brought to King Philip of Macedon. No one could ride it, and the king was about to send it away. His young son Alexander noticed that the horse was afraid of its own shadow. He turned the horse to face the sun, so the shadow fell behind it, calmed it with gentle strokes, and rode it. His father said Macedonia would be too small for him. Alexander grew up to be Alexander the Great.

Write a parallel life. Choose two people you admire, perhaps a grandparent and a hero from a book. Draw a line down a page. On each side, write one story that shows what that person is like. At the bottom, write how they are alike and how they differ. That is what Plutarch did.

full.html: Plutarch (c. AD 46–c. 120) lived all his life in the small town of Chaeronea in central Greece, though he studied at Athens, visited Rome and Egypt, and held the Roman citizenship. For many years he was a priest at Apollo’s temple at Delphi, not far from his home. He wrote a great many essays on ethics, religion and education, later collected as the Moralia, and his most famous work, the Parallel Lives.

The Lives pair a Greek with a Roman: Theseus with Romulus, Lycurgus with Numa, Pericles with Fabius Maximus, Alexander with Julius Caesar, Demosthenes with Cicero, and more. Twenty-two pairs survive, with four single lives; one pair is lost. After most pairs Plutarch adds a short comparison of the two. This rung looks at the Greek side; the next rung looks at the Romans.

full.name: gb-parallel-lives
full.cap: Plutarch’s pairs on a time line. Some lived centuries apart; Plutarch paired them for their character, not their dates.

full.html: At the start of the Life of Alexander, Plutarch explains what he is doing.

full.text: It must be borne in mind that my design is not to write histories, but lives. And the most glorious exploits do not always furnish us with the clearest discoveries of virtue or vice in men: sometimes a matter of less moment, an expression or a jest, informs us better of their characters and inclinations, than the most famous sieges, the greatest armaments, or the bloodiest battles whatsoever. Therefore as portrait-painters are more exact in the lines and features of the face, in which the character is seen, than in the other parts of the body, so I must be allowed to give my more particular attention to the marks and indications of the souls of men.
full.author: Plutarch
full.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
full.ed: Everyman’s Library, J. M. Dent, vol. II

full.html: Plutarch’s method: a life is a moral portrait. He tells the deeds, but he chooses the details, the sayings, habits and small choices, that show what a person was like, so that readers can learn which qualities to copy and which to avoid.
In the Life of Pericles Plutarch says we admire a fine statue without wanting to become a sculptor, but good actions are different: they make us want to act the same way.

full.text: But virtue, by the bare statement of its actions, can so affect men’s minds as to create at once both admiration of the things done and desire to imitate the doers of them.
full.author: Plutarch
full.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
full.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 12, P. F. Collier & Son

items: Lycurgus, Sparta’s lawgiver, whose rules trained citizens in hardship and discipline. Plutarch admits that almost nothing about him is certain.

Solon, who gave Athens fairer laws. Plutarch tells how the rich king Croesus asked Solon who was the happiest man, and Solon would call no one happy until his life had ended well. Plutarch says some doubt the meeting could have happened, but he keeps it because it fits Solon’s character.
Themistocles, who built the fleet that beat the Persians at Salamis in 480 BC, and was later exiled by his own city.

Aristides “the Just.” When Athens voted on exiling him, a farmer who could not write asked him, not knowing who he was, to write “Aristides” on the voting shard. Asked why, the farmer said he was tired of hearing him called “the Just.” Aristides wrote it.
Pericles, who led Athens in its golden age and had the Parthenon built.
Demosthenes, who as a young man trained his weak voice by speaking with pebbles in his mouth, and became Athens’s greatest orator.
Alexander the Great, from the horse Bucephalus to the conquest of Persia.

full.html: One more Alexander story shows Plutarch’s eye for a telling moment. The young king visits the philosopher Diogenes, who lived with almost nothing, and finds him lying in the sun.

full.text: When he kindly asked him whether he wanted anything, “Yes,” said he, “I would have you stand from between me and the sun.” Alexander was so struck at this answer, and surprised at the greatness of the man, who had taken so little notice of him, that as he went away he told his followers, who were laughing at the moroseness of the philosopher, that if he were not Alexander, he would choose to be Diogenes.
full.author: Plutarch
full.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
full.ed: Everyman’s Library, J. M. Dent, vol. II

full.html: Reading Plutarch as a modern historian. He wrote centuries after most of his subjects, used many sources of uneven quality, and sometimes repeats legends because they show character. Historians still use him, but they check him against other evidence. He himself tells readers when a story is doubtful.

items: Shakespeare took the plots of Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus from Sir Thomas North’s English Plutarch (1579), often following North’s wording closely.
Founders and leaders read him for examples: Montaigne loved him, and many of the American founders knew his heroes well.
Biography as we know it, a life told to show a person’s character, owes more to Plutarch than to anyone else.

deep.text: Context: a Greek in a Roman world

deep.html: By Plutarch’s day Greece had been ruled by Rome for two centuries. Pairing the two peoples was a quiet argument: Greece had heroes and lawgivers to set beside any Roman, and the two cultures belonged together. Plutarch had Roman friends of high rank, and he dedicated the Lives to one of them, Sosius Senecio.

items: Can we learn to be good by reading about good people? Or do we copy the exciting bad ones instead?
Is a small habit a truer sign of character than a great deed?
Solon would call no one happy until the end of his life. Was he right?
Is it fair to compare two people who lived centuries apart, in very different worlds?

deep.html: Montaigne, later on this ladder, named Plutarch and Seneca as the two authors he read most. Shakespeare turned Plutarch’s Romans into drama. Boswell’s Life of Johnson, in the 18th-century era of this ladder, took Plutarch’s idea further: a life told through a person’s talk and small habits, day by day.

questions: Plutarch says a joke or a quick answer can show character better than a battle. What small thing someone did once showed you what they were really like?
Alexander saw that the horse feared its shadow. What does that story tell you about him?
Diogenes asked a king only to step out of his sunlight. Why did Alexander admire him for that?
Why might the farmer have been tired of hearing Aristides called “the Just”? Is it easy to like someone who is always praised?
Whose life would you want written down as an example? Whose as a warning?
